subject: Architecture
title: Hagia Sophia: From Church to Mosque to Museum
description: A 60-second lesson on Hagia Sophia: From Church to Mosque to Museum.

hook.text: Hagia Sophia has been a church, a mosque, and a museum — and now it's a mosque again.

buildup.text: Emperor Justinian built it in just five years — completed in 537 AD in Constantinople, now Istanbul.

discovery.text: Its dome floats 180 feet above the floor on a ring of 40 windows. Light makes it seem suspended from heaven.

twist.text: When the Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453, they added minarets but preserved the Christian mosaics.

climax.text: For nearly 1,000 years it had the world's largest dome — inspiring every major religious building after it.

punchline.text: Two religions. Three identities. One building that changed architecture.

quiz.question: How long did Hagia Sophia hold the record for the world's largest dome?

details.summary: Hagia Sophia has served as a Byzantine cathedral (537-1453), Ottoman mosque (1453-1934), museum (1934-2020), and mosque again (2020-present). Each transformation added architectural layers — minarets, buttresses.
details.whyItMatters: Hagia Sophia demonstrates that sacred buildings outlive the civilizations that create them. Its repeated conversions show how sacred architecture absorbs new meanings across centuries.
takeaways: Served as church, mosque, museum, and mosque again over 1,500 years
Each conversion added layers — minarets, calligraphy, buttresses
A living palimpsest where multiple faiths share the same walls

faq.question: Are Christian mosaics still visible inside?
faq.answer: Some are. When converted to a mosque in 1453, many mosaics were plastered over rather than destroyed. The museum period (1934-2020) uncovered several magnificent examples. After reconversion to a mosque in 2020, some mosaics are covered during prayer times but remain preserved beneath.

faq.question: Why does Hagia Sophia have such massive buttresses?
faq.answer: The 31-meter dome exerts enormous outward thrust on its supports. The original structure experienced partial dome collapse in 558 CE. Successive Byzantine and Ottoman engineers added progressively larger buttresses to stabilize the building.
